opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of people hear "follow the mainstream" and assume it means giving up on originality. For frontier-model research, I see it almost the other way around.

At the frontier, the mainstream isn't just a fashion. It's where the whole field has put its compute, data, engineering effort and collective attention. When thousands of very smart people and a huge amount of resources converge on one direction, like scaling pretraining, then reinforcement learning on reasoning, then agents, that direction usually reflects some real signal about what works. If you stay close to it, you're standing on the strongest foundation available, and your work connects to everything else happening. People can build on it, compare against it, and you can absorb their progress just as fast.

The second reason is practical. Frontier research is extremely expensive, and the feedback loops are long. If you go off on a very niche path, you might spend months on something that never scales, or that gets made irrelevant by the next general improvement in the base model. That happens a lot. Many clever tricks from a few years ago simply disappeared once models got stronger. Following the mainstream is partly a way of not betting against the "bitter lesson."

But the key point is that following the mainstream doesn't mean copying. The real innovation at the frontier often happens inside the mainstream: making training more efficient, finding a better architecture detail, solving a stability problem at scale, getting the data right. These look like small, unglamorous things, but at scale they compound into very large differences. A lot of the impact comes from doing the mainstream thing extremely well and extremely deeply, more than anyone else, until you see something others haven't noticed yet.

So for me the logic is: first get fully into the main current, understand it at the level of engineering detail, and make sure you can actually reproduce and push the frontier. Then, from that position, you have the judgment to know which deviations are worth making. Innovation from inside the mainstream tends to be much more grounded than innovation from outside it.

r001.rationale: The response says resources and attention converge on shared research directions, but does not explain that inference and hardware development are coordinated around the same goal.

r002.rationale: It says small, unglamorous improvements compound at scale into large differences, describing cumulative advances in frontier research.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think "following the mainstream" sounds almost like a bad thing to say, because in research we're always told to be original, to find the niche nobody else has found. But in frontier-model work, I've come to believe the opposite is closer to the truth.

The reason is that the mainstream is where the signal is. When you look at what the strongest labs are converging on, whether that's the transformer, scaling laws, RLHF, mixture-of-experts, or long-context training, that convergence is not an accident. Hundreds of very smart people with enormous compute have tried the alternatives, and the mainstream is the residue of all of that selection. If you insist on going against it, you're essentially betting that you alone have seen something that all of them missed. Occasionally that bet pays off, but most of the time it just means you spend a year and a lot of GPUs rediscovering why something doesn't work.

So the way I think about it is this: the mainstream tells you which problems are real and which directions have gradient. Your job as a researcher is not to find a different mountain, it's to climb the same mountain faster or to find a better path up it. The differentiation comes from execution, from details, from the thousands of small decisions in data, in training stability, in evaluation, that the published papers never fully describe. That's where real competitive advantage lives.

There's also a very practical point. Frontier-model research is incredibly expensive, and you can't afford to run many independent experiments at full scale. Aligning with the mainstream lets you borrow validation from the whole community. You can take it as mostly settled that a certain architecture or recipe scales, and spend your scarce compute on the parts that are genuinely uncertain for you. If you reject the mainstream, you have to pay for all of that validation yourself.

And finally, following the mainstream keeps you honest. It forces you to compare against the best, on the same benchmarks, with the same expectations. It's very easy to feel innovative in a corner where no one else is looking. It's much harder, and much more meaningful, to be slightly better than everyone in the place where everyone is looking.

So I don't see it as a lack of ambition. I see it as respecting the accumulated judgment of the field, and then putting all of your creativity into the places where that judgment hasn't settled yet.

astra-6.text:
I think following the mainstream helps you understand where the frontier actually is. When many researchers are working within the same framework, their results give you a foundation: you can compare approaches, learn what works, and see which problems remain unresolved.

That doesn’t mean you should assume the mainstream is always right. But if you want to challenge an approach, you need to understand why it works and where it breaks down. Otherwise, it’s easy to mistake being different for making progress.

For me, the value is in building that understanding, then developing your own judgment about what to pursue. Working on a mainstream problem can put you in a better position to notice something others have overlooked.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is what you mean by following the mainstream. For me, it means understanding the strongest methods deeply enough to know why they work, where they fail, and which assumptions haven’t really been tested.

Frontier-model research is very empirical. If you haven’t reproduced a strong baseline, it’s difficult to tell whether your new idea is an improvement or whether you’re just comparing against something that wasn’t working properly. Working with the mainstream gives you that foundation and a shared language for discussing results.

But you shouldn’t stop there. You follow it to reach the boundary of what’s known. Then you can make a more informed judgment about where to depart from it. The goal is to develop independent judgment through that process.
